newsitem.title: USA: IRS urged at hearing to revoke yield burning plan.
newsitem.headline: IRS urged at hearing to revoke yield burning plan.

text.p: Municipal bond issuers, lawyers and dealers implored the IRS at a public hearing on Wednesday to revoke a controversial "yield burning" ruling that could cost localities millions of dollars in penalities.

The $1.3 trillion municipal bond market has been rocked by allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond refinancing transactions, a practice dubbed yield burning.
Wednesday's hearing may be the last formal opportunity that bond groups have to comment on a controversial "closing agreement" plan that the Internal Revenue Service announced last year.

The plan says issuers can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by paying Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest.

But angry bond lawyers and issuers charged at the hearing that IRS's plan is unfair and exorbitantly expensive for localities. They said the underwriters that sold inflated Treasury securities should be stuck with the bill.
"It's as if the victim of theft is being penalized for allowing itself to being robbed," William Conner, representing the National Association of Bond Lawyers, told the six-member IRS hearing panel.

Conner charged that IRS was well aware in the early 1990s that bond issuers routinely bought Treasury securities without getting competitive bids or detailed written explanations from underwriters about why they thought the Treasuries were purchased at fair market value.
Asked by today's panel why issuers did not press underwriters for written explanations, NABL's Connor said dealers refused to provide them for proprietary reasons.
Conner told IRS that the revenue procedure is unneeded because Section 6700 of the IRS code already gives the Service the ammunition it need to pursue yield burning violators.
The rule says IRS can fine anyone that aids or abets tax fraud. The fine is $1,000 per denomination, bond lawyers say.

A Government Finance Officers Association spokesman said the group is "outraged" by IRS' revenue procedure. Art Heilman, Pennsylvania's director of revenue, said issuers feel "exasperation and frustration" at having to pay the bills.

Heilman also asked why the National Association of Securities Dealers is not enforcing more aggressively its rules barring excessive price markups in Treasuries. And why is the Securities and Exchange Commission not pressing NASD on the subject, he asked.
Bond dealers also urged IRS to withdraw its "one size fits all" ruling.

George Brakatselos, vice president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said a recent study that priced 104 advance refunding escrows and concluded that issuers nationwide face a combined liability of as much as $1 billion is "fundamentally flawed."

For instance, he said the study, prepared for the lawfirm Phillips & Cohen, uses Wall Street Journal prices as a benchmark to calculate alleged markups. Such prices are at best only "rough indicators" of market price, he said.
Phillips & Cohen represents the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which has filed yield-burning charges against its former financial advisor, Lazard Freres & Co.

L.A. transportation official Terry Massumoto, urged the federal government to put the revenue procedure on hold until the SEC and Justice Dept. have fully investigated possible wrongdoing by Wall Street firms.
